analysis.one_liner: Creates a government health service providing free, comprehensive health care to everyone in the United States, funded by income taxes.
analysis.headline: A universal, free government health care bill never got a hearing: it sat in three House committees and their subcommittees from June 2005 until the Congress ended in January 2007, with only 11 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced America's mix of private insurance, employer plans, Medicare and Medicaid with a single government-run health service. Every person in the United States would get doctor visits, hospital care, dental, vision, mental health, prescription drugs, ambulance rides and home care at no charge, delivered by salaried government health workers in Service facilities. It would be paid for by a new tax on individual and corporate income, and private health insurers, for-profit hospitals and other companies now paid for health care would see that business end.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone in the United States, including the roughly 40 million uninsured cited in the bill's findings, would get comprehensive care with no premiums, deductibles or bills. Workers would gain a right to paid leave for medical care, and the bill targets underserved rural, inner-city, migrant, prison and minority populations for extra resources. Health workers would get federal civil-service jobs, union rights including the right to strike, and student loan repayment.

how_it_helps.text: Makes every individual in the United States eligible for free comprehensive health services, including doctor care, hospital care, dental, vision, mental health, long-term care, prescriptions, ambulance transportation and child care during appointments.
The bill's own findings state the existing system failed to cover more than forty million Americans and that unnecessary profits and administrative expenses had inflated health care costs.
Adds a right to paid leave under the Fair Labor Standards Act: workers earn one hour of paid health leave for every 35 hours worked, usable for their own or a dependent's care.

Requires the National Health Board to redistribute resources to underserved populations, with governing bodies at local and regional levels majority-controlled by users of the system and an Inspector General to investigate grievances.

Gives Service employees federal labor-law coverage, permits strikes, mandates union representation by card-check rather than election, and pays up to 100% of student loans for four years of Service employment.

analysis.who_pays: A new tax on individual and corporate income funds the Health Service Trust Fund. Private health insurers lose their entire market; for-profit hospitals, clinics and managed-care companies lose their business model; drug and device makers would sell to a government formulary with government-set rules; and physicians and other providers would become salaried employees barred from private fees. Workers whose employers currently provide coverage would be moved into the government system.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and their subcommittees from June 2005 until the Congress ended in January 2007, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies that profit from the existing system — private health insurers, for-profit hospitals, managed care and drug makers — kept their markets untouched, and the roughly 40 million uninsured of 2005 remained without coverage for the rest of the decade until a narrower law passed in 2010.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and for-profit providers

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 20, 2005 and gave introductory remarks on it in May 2006.

for.name: 11 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor ever joined, and the bill never moved in committees chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill replaces private health insurance with a public service, ending the industry's market. Its own transition section sets aside retraining funds for displaced health-insurance-industry workers. Insurers' interest in keeping the status quo ran directly against the uninsured.

Care would be delivered through government facilities by salaried workers, and the bill's findings blame 'unnecessary and excessive profits' and for-profit managed care for inflated costs. The bill would end for-profit delivery of most care.

Prescriptions would be filled through a National Pharmacy and Medical Supply Formulary the government publishes and controls, ending much of the pricing power the industry has under private insurance and Medicare Part D.

Providers would become salaried federal employees barred from private fees, losing independent-practice income, but they would gain civil-service protections, union rights, hiring preference, and full student loan repayment for Service employment.
Eyeglasses, hearing aids, prosthetics and other devices would be supplied through the government formulary at negotiated terms, replacing private-market sales.
